opus-5.5.text:
Well, I want to be careful here, because I don't think it's *usually* bad. But there's a specific worry I take seriously.

When people in the AI safety world talk about "giving governments options," they often mean developing the policy ideas, the technical infrastructure, the expertise so that if a government decides it wants to act, it can act well. That sounds strictly good: more options, better decisions. But options don't get used in a vacuum. Governments aren't neutral optimizers picking the best item off a menu. They're responding to political pressures, to national security framings, to whatever the dominant narrative is at the moment.

So one concern is that some of the most "actionable" options you build end up being the ones that accelerate things you didn't want. If the frame in Washington is "we need to beat China," then the tools you've built for, say, tracking compute or coordinating with labs could get repurposed toward a race dynamic, toward nationalizing development in a way that speeds it up, or toward tightening control over AI by a small number of actors. You thought you were building safety infrastructure, and it became racing infrastructure.

A second concern is about premature lock-in. If you hand a government a fairly developed regulatory regime before we really understand the risks, it might get adopted in a form that's mostly symbolic, or aimed at the wrong things, and then that becomes the thing everyone points to as "AI is regulated now." That can make it harder to do the right thing later, when we know more.

And a third is just that the people developing options often have more influence over *which* options exist than over *how they're used*. That asymmetry should make you humble. You're kind of loading a toolbox for someone whose goals you only partly share.

None of this means we shouldn't do policy work. I think we should, and a lot of it is really valuable. But I'd push people to ask, for any given option: in the hands of a government under racing pressure, with mixed motives, does this tend to make things safer, or does it just make things *faster* or more concentrated? Some options are pretty robustly good — things like better evaluations, transparency requirements, the capacity to understand what's going on inside labs. Others are much more double-edged, and I think people sometimes treat "more government capacity" as uniformly good when it really isn't.

r001.rationale: The response says governments may have mixed motives or respond to racing pressure, but does not identify future leaders using granted powers against the goals behind them.

r002.rationale: It describes some options as double-edged and warns they may concentrate control, but gives no chance approaching 50% that centralising policy interventions will be harmful.

r003.rationale: It discusses how political narratives and uncertainty about risks can shape policy, but does not say that perceived tractability of AI alignment research shapes government policy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've gone back and forth on a lot, and I want to be careful here because I don't think the answer is obvious. The naive view is that more options is always better — if you're a government and you have a wider menu of things you could do about AI, you can pick the best one. And in some abstract sense that's true. But I think there are a few ways it can go wrong in practice.

The first one is just that governments don't necessarily pick the best option. A lot of the work in AI policy that people in my world have been excited about is basically creating capabilities — building the technical ability to measure what models can do, to track where the compute is, to verify what labs are doing. And the hope is that those capabilities get used for things like, "let's make sure nobody deploys a system that could help with a bioweapon." But once you've built the capability, it exists, and it can be used for other things. The ability to track compute is the ability to track compute. The ability to mandate evaluations is the ability to mandate whatever evaluations the government of the day cares about. So you have to ask not just "would a thoughtful policymaker use this well?" but "what's the distribution of people who are going to have their hands on this lever over the next couple of decades?"

The second thing is that some options are kind of attractive nuisances. There are interventions that look appealing in the moment — a quick way to look tough, or to get an edge over a rival country — but that make the overall situation worse. And if that option is sitting on the table, there's a decent chance someone picks it up at a bad moment. If you'd never built the tooling for it, you wouldn't have had that risk. I think about this a lot with anything that increases the state's ability to concentrate control over the technology. Even if the version in my head is a sensible safety regime, the version that gets implemented could end up being something that just hands enormous power to whoever's in charge, and that's one of the outcomes I'm most worried about.

And then the third thing, which is a bit more subtle, is that creating options changes the conversation. Once you've shown that it's feasible to do something, you've shifted the window of what's considered a normal thing to propose. Sometimes that's good. But sometimes you've just made it easier for a bad idea to become a serious proposal.

So the way I'd put it is: I don't think "more options" is bad as a default. I still lean toward most of the capacity-building stuff being net positive, because right now governments are often flying pretty blind and that's its own kind of dangerous. But I think people in this space should be asking a harder question than "is this a good tool?" They should be asking "who ends up holding this tool, and what's the worst realistic thing they do with it?" And for some interventions, when you ask that honestly, you might decide not to build it.

r001.rationale: The response warns that capabilities built for safety can later be used by whoever holds government power for other purposes, and asks who will hold the tools over coming decades.

r002.rationale: It describes harmful outcomes as a concern and says there is a “decent chance” of misuse, but does not communicate a likelihood approaching 50%.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that perceived tractability of AI alignment research shapes government AI policy.

astra-6.text:
One worry is that giving governments more options isn’t necessarily the same as making good outcomes more likely. It depends on which options they’re going to choose, and what those options displace.

Suppose you think a fairly strong intervention is needed to reduce risks from AI. If you develop a bunch of more modest interventions, you might hope those are useful steps in the right direction. But they could also give policymakers a way to say, “We’ve dealt with this,” without doing the thing that would actually address the risk. So the modest policy could be a substitute for the stronger policy, rather than a stepping stone toward it.

I don’t think that means we shouldn’t develop policy options. It means that “we’re just giving people more options” isn’t, by itself, a sufficient argument that the work is beneficial. You still need a view about how those options will change what governments actually do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses policymakers using modest interventions as substitutes for stronger ones, but does not identify the risk that future leaders may use granted powers against the goals behind granting them.

r002.rationale: It says modest interventions could displace stronger policy, but does not discuss interventions that shift power centralization or characterize their chance of harm as approaching 50%.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention how perceived tractability of AI alignment from research could shape government policy.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think giving governments more options sounds unambiguously good if you imagine that they’ll carefully consider all of them and pick the best one. But that’s not necessarily how policy works. Attention is limited, and there are political incentives to do something that’s visible and achievable.

So if you give a government ten things it could do about AI, it might pick the three that are easiest to get agreement on, do those, and feel like it’s addressed the problem. And those might not do much about the risks you were most concerned about. They could even make it harder to take more consequential action later, because now people can say, “We already passed the AI bill.”

That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t develop policy options. It means that having more options isn’t automatically progress. You have to think about which actions they’re likely to displace, and whether you’re making it easier for governments to address the problem or just easier to look like they have.

r001.rationale: It discusses political incentives and the risk of settling for visible, low-impact actions, but does not mention future leaders exercising granted powers against the original goals.

r002.rationale: It says more policy options may fail to address key risks or impede later action, but gives no roughly 50% chance estimate and does not discuss interventions that shift centralisation of power.

r003.rationale: It does not connect government AI policy to how tractable AI alignment appears from research.
